High purified magnesium (HP-Mg) with 99.97% purity was used as the substrate material.
Anodization was performed at 30, 50, and 70°C for 2-4 minutes with 4-6 volts (DC) in aqueous electrolytes (50% NaOH, 1 M KOH, and borate benzoate).
The borate benzoate electrolyte was composed of 60 g/L NaOH, 25 g/L Na2B4O7, 20 g/L H3BO3, and 3 g/L NaBz.
The highest water contact angle of 164° was achieved for the coated magnesium anodized at +5 volts for 3 minutes in borate benzoate at 30°C.
The corrosion rate of bare HP-Mg in simulated body fluid (SBF) at 37°C was around 15 mm/year.
The optimum corrosion rate of 12 μm/year was achieved for HP-Mg anodized at +4 volts for 4 minutes at 70°C in borate benzoate, then coated with stearic acid.
Increasing the anodization temperature from 30 to 70°C improved the corrosion resistance, likely due to the formation of a more porous hydroxide/oxide layer.
Polishing the magnesium to 1 μm finish provided 10x and 5x higher corrosion resistance compared to 1200 grit polished samples when anodized at +4 volts for 2 and 3 minutes, respectively.
Changing the stearic acid concentration from 0.05 to 0.15 mol/L had a negligible effect on the corrosion behavior of the coated magnesium.
The protective coating layer was temporary, as the corrosion resistance decreased after 12 hours of immersion in SBF, before partially recovering.
Borate benzoate electrolyte provided the best corrosion resistance when anodized at +4 volts, compared to KOH and NaOH electrolytes.
Increasing the anodizing voltage from 4 to 6 volts and the time from 2 to 4 minutes generally improved the corrosion resistance.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) were used to measure the corrosion rates of the coated and bare magnesium samples.
The corrosion current density from PDP was converted to corrosion rate using the provided equation.
Three specimens were used for each condition to confirm the reproducibility of the EIS and PDP measurements.
